story.title: Michigan Democrats Select Senate Nominee Amid Record Spending and Party Divisions
story.summary: Michigan Democrats are voting in a Senate primary featuring Rep. Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. The race has garnered significant attention due to record financial contributions, particularly from pro-Israel groups, totaling around $30 million. The candidates represent differing views on U.S.-Israel relations and the future direction of the Democratic Party, highlighting a divide within the party.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after Michigan's primary?
explore_lenses.title: The winner advances to a November contest
explore_lenses.summary: The Democratic primary winner will become the party's nominee for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat and proceed to the November 3 general election. On August 4, voting is underway, so early returns are not the same as certified results.

claims.text: Michigan lists August 4, 2026 as its primary-election date and November 3, 2026 as the general-election date.
CBS reported that Republican Mike Rogers was running unopposed for his party's nomination, meaning the Democratic nominee is expected to face him in the general election.
The Michigan Secretary of State has an August 4 results page, but the supplied official material does not establish a final certified Democratic Senate result as of the day of voting.

explore_lenses.label: How do Stevens and El-Sayed differ on Israel?
explore_lenses.title: They offer competing accounts of U.S. support
explore_lenses.summary: Israel policy is a documented point of disagreement, not merely a proxy for party factions. Stevens says she supports a two-state solution and continued military aid, while El-Sayed has called Israel's actions in Gaza genocide and opposes U.S. aid to Israel.

claims.text: Stevens told CBS that she supports a two-state solution, wants peace and dignity for Palestinians and Israelis, and has criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; she also defended continuing U.S. military aid to Israel.
El-Sayed has criticized U.S. aid to Israel and described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide, according to CBS and AP reporting.
Stevens alleges that El-Sayed will not recognize Israel's right to exist; the consulted reporting presents that as her allegation, not as an independently established finding.

explore_lenses.label: What does the AIPAC spending represent?
explore_lenses.title: Outside expenditures, not $30 million donated to Stevens
explore_lenses.summary: The widely cited roughly $30 million is reported spending by AIPAC and affiliated groups backing Stevens, chiefly through independent political activity. It should not be conflated with a direct contribution to her campaign, and totals may move as late spending reports are filed.

claims.text: AP reported that AIPAC and affiliated groups had spent close to $30 million backing Stevens, describing it as their largest investment in a single race.

The FEC classifies United Democracy Project, an AIPAC-affiliated group identified in reporting on the race, as an independent-expenditure-only super PAC; the FEC says such spending is not money directly given to or spent by the candidate.

El-Sayed argues that AIPAC's role has distorted the contest, while Stevens says she wants to end dark money and argues that her support reflects Democratic backing rather than a reason to change her position.
The FEC cautions that newly filed summary data may take up to 48 hours to appear, so an exact final outside-spending total cannot be fixed from the consulted records on election day.

story_report.summary: Michigan Democrats are voting to choose a Senate nominee between Rep. Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed in a contest shaped by sharp differences over U.S. policy toward Israel and heavy outside political spending. The winner is expected to advance to the Nov. 3 general election against Republican Mike Rogers, who CBS reported was unopposed for his party’s nomination. Michigan lists Aug. 4 as the primary date, but the supplied official material does not establish a final certified Democratic Senate result on the day of voting.

sections.heading: Israel Policy Divides Democratic Candidates
sections.body: Stevens told CBS she supports a two-state solution, seeks peace and dignity for Palestinians and Israelis, and has criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. She also defended continued U.S. military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has criticized that aid and described Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide, according to CBS and AP. Stevens has alleged that El-Sayed would not recognize Israel’s right to exist, but the reporting presents that as her allegation rather than an independently established finding.

sections.heading: AIPAC-Linked Spending Shapes Contest
sections.body: AP reported that AIPAC and affiliated groups had spent close to $30 million backing Stevens, calling it their largest investment in a single race. The FEC classifies United Democracy Project, an AIPAC-affiliated group identified in reporting on the contest, as an independent-expenditure-only super PAC, meaning its spending is not money directly given to or spent by a candidate. El-Sayed says AIPAC’s role distorted the race, while Stevens says she wants to end dark money and that Democratic support does not require her to change her position.

unresolved.text: Election-night results can change as ballots are tabulated and canvassed, and a projected winner should not be treated as a certified nominee.
An exact final outside-spending total remains unsettled because FEC summary data can take up to 48 hours to appear and reported totals vary by cutoff date and by which supporting groups are counted.

related_stories.title: Blanche Gains GOP Support by Abandoning Controversial Fund
related_stories.summary: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has secured support from two Republican senators who previously opposed his nomination. This shift follows his commitment to eliminate a $1.8 billion 'anti-weaponization' fund, which was intended for settlements to Trump allies, including those involved in the January 6 events.

related_stories.summary: Voters in five states—Michigan, Virginia, Missouri, Kansas, and Washington—are heading to the polls for primary elections. Key races include House battlegrounds and party contests, alongside the influence of Donald Trump. Observers are particularly focused on the Democratic Senate showdown in Michigan and other significant contests in the participating states.

related_stories.title: Jeanine Pirro Meets Trump Amid Future Uncertainty
related_stories.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro met with President Trump at the White House, raising questions about her future following his criticism of her handling of the Reflecting Pool vandalism cases. Trump expressed disappointment, stating she 'choked' in her decisions, but sources indicate her position remains secure for now.
